newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran blasts U.S. attack as Clinton election ploy.
newsitem.headline: Iran blasts U.S. attack as Clinton election ploy.

text.p: Iranian state radio blasted U.S. cruise missile attacks against Iraqi targets on Tuesday as electionering by President Bill Clinton.

"Since Clinton is in the run-up to an election, he has found an attack on Baghdad to be the most convenient way of projecting a powerful image of himself and decreasing the pressure from the rival (Republican) party," Tehran radio said in a commentary.
The United States had also attacked Iraq to "uphold its prestige and international standing," the radio added.
Washington on Tuesday launched missile strikes against air defence targets in southern Iraq in retaliation for Iraqi military attacks against Kurdish groups, the Pentagon said.
The radio also slammed Iraqi President Saddam Hussein for his "new adventurism...which once again provided America with an excuse to attack Iraq".
Iran, at war with Iraq from 1980 to 1988, remained neutral in the 1990-1991 Gulf conflict. It denounced Baghdad's invasion of Kuwait as well as the U.S.-led Gulf War.
The radio said Washington had acted in self-interest by not preventing the Iraqi incursion into Kurdish areas and by not reacting to it earlier.

"America did not show much of a reaction at the start of Iraq's attack to remind Iraqi Kurdish groups of its role in ensuring the security of the northern region and also to pressure these groups to accept its mediation plans," it added.
The radio was referring to U.S.-mediated peace talks between the two Kurdish factions which broke down in London last week.
Iran has blasted the U.S. mediation, saying Washington was trying to gain influence in northern Iraq by countering Tehran's diplomatic efforts there.
Iran on Monday blamed the United States for the crisis in northern Iraq and said the conflict could only be resolved through peaceful means and without interference by powers from outside the region.
In a statement issued hours before the U.S. attack on Iraq, a Foreign Ministry spokesman said military action could spark an Iraqi refugee exodus towards Iranian borders as in 1991.
Some 1.3 million Iraqis, most of them Kurds, fled to Iran when Baghdad crushed Kurdish and Shi'ite Moslem uprisings which erupted after Iraq's defeat in the Gulf War.
The spokesman also denied Iran was involved in the conflict.
He was responding to claims by Baghdad and the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) that Tehran was backing the rival Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK).
Tehran also warned Iranian Kurdish rebel groups based in northern Iraq against launching any cross-border raids.
"If the borders of the Islamic Republic of Iran are violated from Iraqi territory by counter-revolutionary elements, we would strongly deal with it," the spokesman said.
Iranian troops in July attacked positions of an Iranian Kurdish opposition group in northern Iraq after Tehran accused the rebels of cross-border attacks.
